title: What Actually Happens When You Hit Send on an Email?
sources: Akamai, 'Quick Guide to SMTP' and Univ. of Tartu sysadmin notes 'Email (SMTP, IMAP, POP3)': the mail client submits the message to an outgoing SMTP server; that server looks up the MX record of the recipient's domain (the part after @) in DNS, delivers the message over SMTP to the recipient's mail server, where it is stored in the mailbox until the recipient's client fetches it with IMAP or POP3
Kaspersky Securelist, 'Spam and phishing in 2025': 44.99% of all emails sent worldwide were spam

Wikipedia, 'Ray Tomlinson' (citing NPR / Tomlinson interviews): in 1971 he sent the first networked email, a test message between two computers placed side by side; he chose @ to separate user from host because the symbol was not used in usernames

lines.text: What actually happens when you hit send on an email?
lines.caps: WHAT ACTUALLY *HAPPENS | WHEN YOU HIT *SEND | ON AN *EMAIL?

lines.text: Well, your app hands it to a sending server,
lines.caps: WELL YOUR *APP | HANDS IT TO A | *SENDING SERVER

lines.text: which reads the part after the at sign, like gmail dot com.
lines.caps: WHICH READS THE *PART | AFTER THE *@ SIGN | LIKE *GMAIL.COM

lines.text: Then it asks DNS, the internet's phone book,
lines.caps: THEN IT ASKS *DNS | THE INTERNET'S | *PHONE BOOK

lines.text: which server takes mail for that name.
Your server passes it across the internet,
and it waits in their mailbox until their phone pulls it down.
lines.caps: AND IT *WAITS | IN THEIR *MAILBOX | UNTIL THEIR *PHONE | *PULLS IT DOWN

lines.text: But almost half of all emails are spam,
so filters check each one first.
The twist? The first email, in nineteen seventy-one,
went between two computers sitting side by side,
lines.caps: WENT BETWEEN TWO *COMPUTERS | SITTING SIDE BY *SIDE

lines.text: and its inventor picked the at sign
because nobody used it in names.
